1. Scope

Construct one independent internal space with a solved standing wave and a persistent signed readout proposed as electric charge. The system is a two-component real field on a fixed-end internal interval.

  • Specify geometry, state domain, dynamics, boundaries, sign and normalization.
  • Derive the current and energy balances; exhibit positive, negative and occupied-neutral states; prove the stated isolated stability.
  • List all constants, anchors and degeneracies, then supply a fully numerical example and a work/current exchange interface.

This construction does not require a combined attribute space, a quantum wave equation, a probability postulate or a complete electromagnetic force law. The physical identification of the signed invariant with electric charge is stated explicitly.

Question and constructed result

Construct one internal space whose standing waves provide a signed quantity proposed as electric charge. The construction uses one bounded internal interval carrying a two-component real field. The interval supplies the standing profile; an oriented plane of field values supplies clockwise or counterclockwise motion. The action derived from the selected dynamics has a conserved signed rotation quantity.

The physical identification used in this document is , with a charge-per-action calibration. That identification is stated as premise P5. The calculations establish the geometry, waves, conserved , its charge readout under P5, and their energy and stability properties.

The scope has a mathematical endpoint: derive persistence and the sharp energy bound from the selected dynamics, while retaining the electric identification as its own premise.

The proofs are Q-04 and Q-09; the assumptions are P1–P6, and the actual tests are V02, V04 and V08. The equality cases and neutral preparation are calculated, rather than included in the premises.

This construction does not require their completion. Spatial localization in ordinary space and a relation between the internal clock and another observer's clock are not constructed here.

Assumptions that may not be imported

No quantum wave equation, probability rule, canonical commutator, elementary-charge spectrum, Planck-scale admission law, fixed particle inventory or combined attribute space is used. No internal speed is set equal to the speed of light. The energy assigned to this charge subsystem is not silently identified with a complete particle's rest energy.

Work backward from a persistent signed readout to a suitable internal symmetry, then calculate forward from the specified action. The finite route fixes the geometry, solves its wave equation, derives both local balances, checks sign and stability, and evaluates numerical anchors.

Mathematical operations in the plan

Variation supplies the evolution; an actual symmetry supplies the conserved readout. These are different operations on the same action.

Here the quarter-turn map and canonical momentum are explicitly defined in Appendix P2 and §10.1. The final multiplication by the calibrated constant in P5 assigns charge units. The complete route is checked in V01–V04.

Thought experiments that implement the equations

The fixed-node experiment. Pick a point along the internal interval. Its field value has two real components. In a circular preparation those components trace a circle over time, while the nodes along the interval remain fixed. The circle is in the field-value plane; it is not an orbit in ordinary space. Compare a second preparation with the opposite direction around that circle and the same radius and frequency. The calculated energy is equal and the signed rotation quantity has the opposite sign.

The neutral experiment. Move the field value back and forth along one line in the same plane. Choose its amplitude to give the same energy as the circular state. Its signed rotation quantity is zero throughout, although the wave and its energy are nonzero.

The calibration experiment. Measure an identified mode frequency. It fixes the ratio of internal speed to interval length. It cannot by itself tell whether the internal interval is larger and the internal wave proportionally faster. An independent length or speed anchor is required to separate those possibilities.

These experiments use the same geometry and dynamics. They explain the calculations below rather than replace them.

Appendix P1 — The interval geometry and its scale

Start with the selected compact interval and positive line metric. Under , , so the metric and measure become and . Thus using the unit interval does not remove the length parameter; it moves that parameter into the metric.

The metric coefficient is constant. In this coordinate its connection coefficient is zero, and the one-dimensional intrinsic Riemann curvature vanishes. Fixed-end eigenfunctions derived in §10 have . This is how the selected geometry enters the spectrum.

The coordinate conversion and flatness statements are explicit:

Neither boundedness nor conservation selects . The inverse anchor relation in §12 is the supplied determination procedure.

Trace: Premise P1 → scope obligation O1 → test V01. The related equation groups appear in §6.

Appendix P2 — The oriented value plane and a signed quantity

For vectors , the metric supplies , while the orientation supplies . The first is symmetric; the second changes sign when the oriented order reverses.

A rigid rotation preserves both the metric and orientation form. The quarter-turn tensor acts as , giving . In the action's canonical variables this becomes the rotation quantity .

The load-bearing orientation identity is

Within this bilinear mechanism, a single real component has no nonzero antisymmetric two-index form. The two-component plane therefore supplies the missing oriented motion. This argument concerns this selected mechanism; it does not rule out other charge constructions.

A passive reflected coordinate basis must also transform . Holding the physical orientation fixed while actively reflecting the field is a different operation and reverses , as calculated in §11.

Trace: Premise P2 → scope obligation O3 → test V05. The related equation groups appear in §6.

Appendix P3 — Selected dynamics, variation and isotropy

The selected local action retains the lowest quadratic terms in time and internal-space derivatives, with equal component coefficients and no preferred value-plane direction. This is a sufficient dynamics choice. It is not forced by the interval alone.

Endpoint terms vanish for the stipulated variations. Therefore its stationary trajectories obey Q-03. The canonical energy is a positive sum of squares, Q-05.

The isotropy condition has a checkable role. If one adds a potential with unequal component coefficients, , then

Consequently is not generally conserved in that changed model. Equal coefficients eliminate this torque term; it is not enough merely to name a variable “charge.”

Trace: Premise P3 → scope obligation O2 → test V01. The related equation groups appear in §6.

Appendix P4 — Fixed ends close the balances

For the smooth worked states, at each fixed endpoint for all , so there. The explicit charge and energy fluxes consequently vanish:

For general finite-energy data, conservation follows by convergence of the sine expansion in the energy norm. No pointwise endpoint trace of an arbitrary velocity is assumed.

The chosen boundary conditions break translation symmetry along the interval. No conserved internal translational momentum is claimed. The current being derived is the internal rotation current, whose symmetry survives the fixed ends.

The action dimension of follows from its formula. Multiplication by , with units charge/action, yields a quantity in charge units. Because is constant, the derived balance for becomes the corresponding balance for .

The nonzero circular solution supplies . For a reference orientation with , the explicit calibration inverse is

Appendix P6 — Admissible states and the stability inequality

The sine expansion of a fixed-end finite-energy field is . Orthogonality gives

This proves the inequality used in §11 directly for the selected domain. The modal evolution and conserved sums make the finite-energy extension explicit:

The initial field and velocity determine each modal oscillator uniquely. The positive energy sum controls convergence for all times, and the second bound makes the total signed action well defined. Finite sine sums are smooth worked states; their limits give the stated energy-domain solution and conserved accounts. 8. Summary of the first seven sections for three readers

For a child

We chose a small internal line with two ends. At every place, the field has two numbers. Those numbers can go around a circle while the wave’s nodes stay still. One direction gives a positive reading, the other a negative one; back-and-forth motion gives zero even while the wave has energy.

The three examples have equal energy. We proved that the signed reading stays fixed when nothing enters or leaves, and checked the calculations. The circle is a picture of two field values, not a tiny object orbiting in ordinary space.

For a physics teacher

A fixed-end interval supports two ordinary sine standing-wave components. Their relative phase produces elliptical field-value motion. The action’s rigid internal-rotation symmetry supplies a signed Noether quantity, with a separate declared calibration for the proposed electric readout.

Explicit local currents close at the ends. The lowest circular mode attains the fixed-charge energy bound, and difference solutions conserve the perturbation-energy norm. The opening sections identify the premises, dependencies, numerical anchors and actual pass results.

For a theoretical physicist

The selected model is a real two-component Dirichlet wave with an oriented Euclidean value plane and coercive conserved energy. Its internal rotation symmetry supplies the signed generator; no spatial-rotation identification is assigned to that symmetry.

The sine spectrum, completed-square and Poincaré argument, and conserved difference norm establish the stated results. Calibration exposes scale and normalization degeneracies; the affine log-anchor map gives exact log-covariance propagation when the covariances exist. The endpoint includes a fully specified numerical fixture and exchange identities.

8.1 For a child

We chose a small internal line with two ends. At every place on that line, the field has two numbers. Those numbers can trace a circle as time passes, even though the wave's nodes stay in the same places. Turning around the circle one way gives a positive reading; turning the other way gives a negative reading. Moving back and forth along a line gives a zero reading, even while the wave still has energy.

We wrote down the rules before calculating what happens. Those rules tell us how the field moves and how much energy it has. We then proved that the signed reading stays the same when nothing is sent into or out of the internal line. The three worked examples have equal energy. The mathematical tests passed. The table in §7 tells us exactly what was finished and which numbers were chosen for the example.

The picture of a circle describes the field's two values; it does not put a tiny object on a circular track in ordinary space. Calling the signed reading electric charge is one of the model's stated choices.

8.2 For a physics teacher

The construction specifies an internal fixed-end interval and a two-component real field with isotropic quadratic wave dynamics. Each component has an ordinary sine standing-wave profile. Their relative temporal phase produces elliptical motion in the field-value plane. The action's rigid internal-rotation symmetry supplies a signed Noether quantity. A separately declared calibration converts that quantity into the proposed electric readout.

Both charge and energy have explicit local continuity equations and zero endpoint flux. Opposite circular preparations have equal energy and opposite charge; a linearly polarized preparation supplies a nonzero neutral example at the same energy. The perturbation-energy proof establishes stability of the isolated linear evolution, and the lowest circular mode attains the energy minimum at fixed nonzero charge.

The premise register distinguishes geometry and dynamics choices from their consequences. The anchor table explains what a measured frequency would determine, why it would not fix the internal length separately from speed, and what additional data would fix the constants. Completeness is tested by the seven stated obligations, with the actual pass results and calibration status recorded in §7.

8.3 For a theoretical physicist

The selected model is a linear two-component real wave on a fixed Dirichlet interval with an oriented Euclidean value plane. Its positive kinetic and gradient quadratic forms yield a coercive conserved energy on the stated energy space. The global internal rotation symmetry supplies the signed Noether generator; the electric interpretation is the explicit constant multiple in P5. The field-value symmetry has no assigned identification with physical spatial rotations.

The exact sine spectrum and general mode coefficients determine the readout, energy and retained phase data. The all-mode energy bound follows from a completed square and the Dirichlet Poincaré inequality, with lowest-mode circular equality states. Difference solutions conserve the same energy norm, giving the stated isolated linear stability. The anchor map has exact scale and normalization degeneracies; its logarithmic form is affine, so the log-covariance propagation is exact when those covariances exist.

The first seven sections specify the physical roots, derive their consequences, identify the finite-energy domain, link each claim to its premise foundation and report the tests actually run. 15. Mathematical verdict

Under the six stated premises, the construction gives a solved independent internal wave with a conserved signed charge readout, equal-energy positive/negative/occupied-neutral examples, the proved energy bound and isolated stability, explicit numerical anchors and a complete model-unit example.

The established identities supporting the verdict are

The lowest circular modes attain the bound. The positive, negative and occupied-neutral preparations have the exact equal-energy readouts checked in V06 and V15.

Under P1–P6, including the declared electric-readout identification, the constructed internal interval and oriented two-component field support explicit standing waves carrying a signed conserved candidate electric charge. Positive and negative circular states and a nonzero neutral state satisfy the same wave equation with the calculated equal-energy preparations. The local current proves isolated charge conservation; the energy norm proves linear stability; and the lowest circular modes minimize the energy at fixed nonzero charge. The geometry, constants, anchor procedures, separate exchange interface and complete numerical fixture are specified. This conditional construction is complete.
